title: Dependency Injection, Global Filters, and Execution Order
description: Learn how to use dependency injection in filters, register global filters, and control the order in which filters execute.

data.text: Sometimes a filter needs to use a service — for example, a logger or a database repository. You cannot use constructor injection when applying a filter as an attribute, because attributes must have compile-time constant constructors. Instead, ASP.NET Core provides two attributes: **TypeFilter** and **ServiceFilter**.

terms.definition: Creates a new instance of the filter using DI, resolving constructor parameters automatically.
Resolves an already-registered filter type from the DI container.
The scope (Transient, Scoped, Singleton) registered in Program.cs for the filter's dependencies.

data.text: TypeFilter creates the filter instance through the DI container, so constructor parameters are resolved automatically. The filter class does NOT need to be registered in Program.cs — only its dependencies do.

data.title: Filter with a Logging Dependency
data.content: An exception filter that uses a message service to collect error details.

data.text: ServiceFilter is similar but requires the filter itself to be registered in the DI container. This is useful when you want to reuse the same filter instance across multiple requests (if registered as a singleton).

data.title: ServiceFilter Registration and Usage
data.content: Register the filter as a service and apply it with ServiceFilter.

cards.title: TypeFilter
cards.description: Resolves filter dependencies directly from DI without pre-registering the filter.
pros: No need to register filter in DI
Fresh instance per use with Transient or Scoped
cons: Filter type not directly available in DI container

cards.title: ServiceFilter
cards.description: Requires the filter itself to be registered in DI before use.
cons: Must register every filter in Program.cs

data.text: Global filters apply to **every action in every controller** automatically. You register them once in Program.cs, and they run for every request — no attributes needed. Common uses include logging, CORS policies, and response caching.

data.title: Register a Global Action Filter
data.content: Apply a timer filter to all controllers in the application.

data.title: Use Scoped, Not Singleton
data.text: Filters that access HttpContext or per-request state should be registered as Scoped. A Singleton filter would share state across all users, which is almost always wrong for MVC filters.
When multiple filters run, ASP.NET Core follows a strict execution order. Understanding this order helps you debug unexpected behavior and decide where to place your logic.

data.caption: The default order in which filters execute during a request
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[HTTP Request] --> B[Global Filters]
    B --> C[Controller Filters]
    C --> D[Action Filters]
    D --> E[Action Method Executes]
    E --> F[Action Filters - Result]
    F --> G[Result Filters]
    G --> H[Response Sent]
    I[Exception Filters] -.->|exception occurs| H

data.text: By default, filters of the same scope execute in an undefined order. To control this precisely, implement **IOrderedFilter** and set its `Order` property. Filters with lower values run first.

data.title: Custom Order with IOrderedFilter
data.content: Force an action filter to run before a controller-level filter by setting a lower Order value.

data.title: Exercise: Combine Global, Controller, and Action Filters
data.description: Create three separate action filters: a global one that logs every request, a controller-level one that adds a custom header, and an action-level one that measures execution time. Use IOrderedFilter to ensure the global logger runs first, the header filter second, and the timer last.
data.expectedOutcome: Every response includes a custom header and an elapsed-time message, and the global log shows all requests in order.

data.title: Dependency Injection and Global Filters Checklist

items.text: Register filter dependencies in Program.cs using AddScoped or AddTransient.
Use TypeFilter when the filter class does not need to be in DI.
Use ServiceFilter when the filter itself should be registered and reused.
Implement IOrderedFilter when you need precise control over filter sequencing.
Avoid Singleton lifetime for filters that touch HttpContext.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use TypeFilter or ServiceFilter to inject services into filters.
Global filters apply automatically to every action; register them once in Program.cs.
Filters execute in the order: Global → Controller → Action → Result.
Implement IOrderedFilter to control the execution order of same-scope filters.
data.takeaway: You now have the full picture of how filters work, how to configure them with DI, and how to control their execution. Use filters to keep your controllers clean and your cross-cutting concerns centralized.
